Benedikt Aretius
ben'ā-dikt a-rā'shūs
n. (Benedikt Aretius, c. 1505–1574, Bernese professor of theology, commentator and botanist)
Latin Benedictus, blessed; Aretius, a grecised form of his family name Marti, from Greek arete, virtue.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Benedikt Aretius, born Benedikt Marti near Bern, taught Greek and Hebrew and then theology in the Bern academy for most of his life. He wrote commentaries on the whole New Testament that were reprinted for a century and a compact system of divinity, and he was at the same time one of the first serious botanists of the Alps, climbing after plants and publishing a catalogue of them — a combination the dictionary notes with approval, since the book of nature and the book of Scripture were not rivals to him. His sharpest work was doctrinal. When the Italian anti-Trinitarian Valentinus Gentilis was tried at Bern in 1566 and executed, Aretius published the proceedings with a full defence of the doctrine of the Trinity from Scripture, and that treatise is why he is remembered. The dictionary affirms the doctrine without endorsing the penalty: the Confederacy's sword was not the instrument Christ appointed against heresy. “For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one” (1Jo 5:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the Trinity as the union of three persons in one Godhead, and a commentary as a series of comments or annotations.

expand to see more

TRIN'ITY, n. The union of three persons in one Godhead, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

COM'MENTARY, n. A comment; exposition; explanation; a book of annotations on a text.

BOT'ANY, n. That branch of natural history which treats of vegetables.

HER'ESY, n. A fundamental error in religion; an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine.

Modern Corruption

The Bern commentator who defended the Trinity and catalogued Alpine plants.

expand to see more

The anti-Trinitarian case that Aretius answered is not a sixteenth-century curiosity; it is revived in every generation, and its modern form argues that the Trinity is a Greek philosophical imposition on a Hebrew book. The answer Aretius gave is still the answer: the doctrine is not deduced from metaphysics but gathered from the text, from the Word who was with God and was God, from the one name into which the nations are baptised, and from the three that bear record.

The principle to recover is that orthodoxy is defended from Scripture and not by the magistrate's sword, and here the dictionary parts from Bern in 1566 while holding the doctrine Bern was defending. The baptismal formula is the plainest witness and belongs to the church, not the council: “baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19). And eternal life is set in the knowledge of the Father and the Son together: “that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent” (Joh 17:3).

Usage

"“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1) — the ground of the doctrine."

"“in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19) — the church's own witness, not the council's."
